introduction_markdown:
**General Certificate of Education Board - General Certificate of Education Examination. Geography (0750), Paper 3, ADVANCED LEVEL, June 2025. Duration: three and a quarter hours.**

Answer ALL THE THREE QUESTIONS.

Question ONE carries THIRTY-FOUR marks and the rest carry THIRTY-THREE marks each.

In answering questions on this paper, you are encouraged to refer to your own field and practical work where relevant. Credit will be awarded for such references.

Marks will be awarded for well annotated maps and diagrams where these are relevant.

You are reminded of the necessity for good English and orderly presentation in your answers.

Non Programmable Calculators Are Allowed.

Materials required: Topographic map, Graph Paper and Photograph.

questions.enonce_markdown:
(a) Study Table 1 below showing the distribution of settlements in part of the South West Region of Cameroon on a total land area of 50km².

**Table 1: Distribution of Settlements in SW Cameroon.**

| Village | | Nearest neighbour | Distance from nearest neighbour (km) |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Limbe | Bonadikombo | 1.5 |
| 2 | Moliwe | Ombe | 2.0 |
| 3 | Ombe | Moliwe | 2.0 |
| 4 | Mutengene | Mile 14 | 3.0 |
| 5 | Mile 14 | Bolifamba | 3.0 |
| 6 | Bolifamba | Bulu | 1.0 |
| 7 | Bulu | Molyko | 1.0 |
| 8 | Molyko | Bonduma | 1.5 |
| 9 | Bondouma | Great Soppo | 1.5 |
| 10 | Great Soppo | Bokwango | 2.0 |
| 11 | Bokwango | Tole | 2.0 |

Source: Hypothetical

(i) Calculate the mean distance between the neighbours. (4 marks)

(ii) Using the Nearest Neighbour Index (Rn) formula stated as:

$$
Rn = 2\bar{d}\sqrt{\frac{n}{A}}
$$

Where Rn is the Nearest Neighbour Index, $\bar{d}$ = the mean distance, n = the number of points or settlements and A = the total surface area.

Calculate the Nearest Neighbour Index for this distribution of settlements. (6 marks)

(iii) Outline TWO significance and TWO limitations of the Nearest Neighbour Index (4 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**(a)(i) Mean distance (4 marks).**

Formula: $\bar{d} = \dfrac{\sum d}{n}$ (1 mark), where $\sum d$ is the sum of the nearest-neighbour distances and $n$ the number of settlements.

Sum (1 mark): $1.5 + 2.0 + 2.0 + 3.0 + 3.0 + 1.0 + 1.0 + 1.5 + 1.5 + 2.0 + 2.0 = 20.5$ km, with $n = 11$ villages (1 mark).

$$
\bar{d} = \frac{20.5}{11} = 1.86\ \text{km} \quad (1\ \text{mark; exactly } 1.8636\ \text{km})
$$

**(a)(ii) Nearest Neighbour Index (6 marks).**

Data (1 mark): $\bar{d} = 1.86$ km, $n = 11$, $A = 50\ \text{km}^2$.

Substitution (2 marks):

$$
Rn = 2 \times 1.8636 \times \sqrt{\frac{11}{50}} = 2 \times 1.8636 \times \sqrt{0.22}
$$

Calculation (2 marks): $\sqrt{0.22} = 0.4690$, so

$$
Rn = 2 \times 1.8636 \times 0.4690 \approx 1.75
$$

(with the rounded mean 1.86 the result is 1.74: both are accepted).

**Interpretation (1 mark).** The index runs from 0 (a completely clustered pattern) through 1 (a random pattern) to 2.15 (a perfectly regular, evenly spaced pattern). A value of **1.75**, well above 1 and approaching 2.15, shows that the villages in this part of the South West Region tend towards a **regular (evenly spaced, dispersed) distribution**.

**(a)(iii) TWO significance and TWO limitations (4 marks, 1 each).**

*Significance*

- It gives a **numerical (objective) measure** of the pattern of settlements, on a scale from 0 to 2.15, instead of a simple visual guess (clustered, random or regular).
- It allows **comparison** between different areas or between different dates for the same area, and it helps to suggest causes (relief, water, roads) and to plan services; it is simple and quick to calculate from a map.

*Limitations*

- The result depends on the **area chosen**: the boundary of the study area (A) changes the index, and settlements near the edge have neighbours outside it (edge effect); a small number of points (here only 11; at least 30 are recommended) makes the result unreliable.
- It uses **straight-line distances only** and treats the surface as uniform: it ignores relief, rivers, roads and land quality, and it measures the pattern but does not explain it; the definition of a "settlement" and measurement errors also affect the result.

questions.enonce_markdown:
(b) After a fieldwork exercise to investigate the relative importance of factors influencing the location of a soap factory in Yaoundé, a frequency table was established as shown below (Table 2).

**Table 2: Frequency table to show the most important factor (that is, the number of times each factor appears)**

| ITEMS | Frequency | Rank | Percentages | In degrees |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1. Raw material | 3 | 3rd | 19 | |
| 2. Power | 1 | 4th | 6 | |
| 3. Labour | 5 | 2nd | 31 | 112 |
| 4. Market | 7 | 1st | 44 | |
| Total | 16 | | 100 | 360 |

(i) Complete the table and represent the data using a pie chart. Let the radius of the circle be 4cm (8 marks)

(ii) From the pie chart, which is the dominant locational factor? Justify your answer. (2 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**(b)(i) Completing the table and drawing the pie chart (8 marks).**

**Step 1 - the missing angles (2 marks).** Each percentage is converted to degrees by multiplying by 3.6 (360 / 100); the printed 112 for labour (31 x 3.6 = 111.6) shows that the rounded percentages are used.

| Items | Frequency | Rank | Percentages | In degrees |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1. Raw material | 3 | 3rd | 19 | 19 x 3.6 = 68.4, so **68** |
| 2. Power | 1 | 4th | 6 | 6 x 3.6 = 21.6, so **22** |
| 3. Labour | 5 | 2nd | 31 | 112 |
| 4. Market | 7 | 1st | 44 | 44 x 3.6 = 158.4, so **158** |
| Total | 16 | | 100 | **360** (68 + 22 + 112 + 158) |

(With the raw frequencies, $\frac{3}{16} \times 360 = 67.5$, $22.5$, $112.5$ and $157.5$, which also total 360: accepted.)

**Step 2 - the pie chart (6 marks).**

- Draw a circle of **radius 4 cm** (diameter 8 cm) with a compass and mark its centre (1 mark).
- Draw a vertical radius from the centre to 12 o'clock and, with a protractor, start with the largest sector and go **clockwise** in decreasing order: Market 158 degrees, Labour 112 degrees, Raw material 68 degrees, Power 22 degrees (3 marks for accurate angles). The last angle must close the circle exactly (the angles total 360 degrees).
- Shade or hatch each sector differently, write the name and percentage in or beside the sectors (the Power sector is narrow, so label it outside with a line), and add a **key** (1 mark).
- Give the chart a **title**, for example "Most important factors in the location of a soap factory, Yaounde", and add the source (Table 2) (1 mark).

![fig-2](gce-al-geography-2025-p3-officiel-cameroun_exercice_2_fig_2.png)

**(b)(ii) The dominant locational factor (2 marks).** The dominant factor is the **market**: its sector is the largest, **158 degrees or 44 per cent (almost half of the circle)**; it was named 7 times out of 16 and is ranked first. The soap factory is therefore located mainly to be close to its customers (in a large city with a big population, good roads and demand) and to reduce the cost of delivering the goods; labour (31 per cent) comes second, while power (6 per cent) is the weakest factor.

*Marks: angles 2; circle and sectors 3; shading, labels and key 1; title 1; dominant factor 1; justification 1.*

(c). Study the table below, which shows the three towns in Cameroon as per population size (2012 population estimate) and answer the questions that follow.

**Table 3: Three towns in Cameroon and their population size (2012 estimate)**

| Name | Population (2023 est.) |
|---|---|
| Yaounde | 2,440,062 |
| Bafoussam | 301,894 |
| Buea | 119,039 |

(i) Using the outline map of Cameroon provided, represent the data using proportional circles. Let 3cm be the maximum circle size. (5 marks)

(ii) State two advantages and two disadvantages of proportional circles? (2 marks)

(iii) Describe any other appropriate technique that can be used to represent the data (2 marks)

![fig-1](gce-al-geography-2025-p3-officiel-cameroun_exercice_2_fig_1.png)

*SEPARATE SHEET (INSERT). MAP FOR QUESTION 2 c(i): outline map of Cameroon with the regional capitals marked by dots and named (Maroua, Garoua, Ngaoundere, Bamenda, Bafoussam, Nkongsamba, Buea, Douala, Yaounde, Bertoua, Ebolowa); the legend "Towns" is a dot.*
questions.corrige_markdown:
**(c)(i) Proportional circles (5 marks).**

**Principle.** The **area** of each circle is proportional to the value, so the **radius is proportional to the square root** of the population.

**Step 1 - the largest circle (1 mark).** Yaounde (2,440,062) is the largest value and gets the maximum size of 3 cm. Taking 3 cm as the **diameter**, its radius is 1.5 cm (if the 3 cm is read as a radius, double every radius below).

**Step 2 - the other radii (2 marks).** $r = 1.5 \times \sqrt{\dfrac{P}{2\,440\,062}}$

| Town | Population | $\sqrt{P / 2\,440\,062}$ | Radius (diameter = 3 cm) | Radius (if 3 cm = radius) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Yaounde | 2,440,062 | 1.000 | 1.50 cm | 3.00 cm |
| Bafoussam | 301,894 | 0.352 | 0.53 cm | 1.06 cm |
| Buea | 119,039 | 0.221 | 0.33 cm | 0.66 cm |

**Step 3 - drawing (2 marks).** Centre each circle on the dot of the town on the outline map (Buea in the south-west, Bafoussam in the west, Yaounde in the centre-south), shade them with the same colour, label each circle with its name and population, and add a **graduated key** (circles of 2,000,000, 1,000,000 and 100,000 inhabitants), a title ("Population of three towns in Cameroon") and the source. Where circles overlap, draw the smaller one on top.

![fig-3](gce-al-geography-2025-p3-officiel-cameroun_exercice_2_fig_3.png)

**(c)(ii) Advantages and disadvantages (2 marks: any two advantages and any two disadvantages, 0.5 each).**

*Advantages*

- The relative size of the towns is seen at a glance, and the map shows both the **location** and the **size** of each town.
- Very large and very small values can be shown on the same map (the square root reduces the difference), and the technique is easy to understand and attractive.

*Disadvantages*

- Circles **overlap** in crowded areas (here the towns of the west and south-west) and may hide the map details or each other.
- It is **difficult to read the exact value** or to judge areas by eye, the radii take time to calculate and draw, and the largest towns dominate the map; it cannot show change or the composition of the population.

**(c)(iii) Another technique (2 marks).** A **located (proportional) bar graph**, or a map with **proportional squares**, can show the data. For bars: choose a vertical scale (for example 1 cm = 500,000 people); then Yaounde = 4.9 cm, Bafoussam = 0.6 cm and Buea = 0.2 cm. Draw one bar of equal width at the position of each town on the outline map, starting from the dot, shade the bars, add the scale, a key and a title (1 mark for the description, 1 mark for the scale and the bar heights). (A divided bar or a simple bar chart on graph paper are also acceptable, but they do not show the location.)

*Marks: part (i) circle sizes 3; location, labels and key 2; part (ii) 2; part (iii) 2.*
